content_voiceover: This is a case report on the R1933X mutation in the MYH9 gene causing May-Hegglin anomaly, a patient who was initially thought to have idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura. The peripheral smear on the left shows a giant platelet, nearly the size of a red cell, alongside a neutrophil containing a pale blue, spindle-shaped cytoplasmic inclusion, a so-called Dohle-like body. The bone marrow smear on the right confirms the same inclusion within a myeloid precursor. This combination, macrothrombocytopenia plus neutrophil inclusions, is the morphologic signature that separates MYH9-related disease from ITP, since ITP never produces leukocyte inclusions. MYH9 encodes nonmuscle myosin heavy chain IIA, essential for normal platelet budding from megakaryocytes, and mutations cause an autosomal dominant spectrum, historically split into May-Hegglin anomaly, Sebastian syndrome, Fechtner syndrome, and Epstein syndrome, the latter two also featuring nephritis, sensorineural deafness, and cataracts. Recognizing the smear findings avoids unnecessary steroids or IVIG.
keypoints: MYH9 gene, nonmuscle myosin IIA, autosomal dominant
Giant platelets + neutrophil Dohle-like inclusion bodies
Inclusions absent in ITP - key differentiator
Spectrum: May-Hegglin, Sebastian, Fechtner, Epstein syndromes
keypoint_voiceover: MYH9-related disease is an autosomal dominant disorder of nonmuscle myosin heavy chain IIA. Look for the smear pair, giant platelets plus pale blue Dohle-like inclusions inside neutrophils, a finding never seen in ITP. The clinical spectrum spans May-Hegglin, Sebastian, Fechtner, and Epstein syndromes, with Fechtner and Epstein additionally causing nephritis, sensorineural deafness, and cataracts.
